Woven cloth consists of crossing sets of yarn. Warp yarns extend along the length of the fabric, while weft yarns pass across its width. A loom keeps the warp under tension and provides a way to pass the weft through alternating openings. The arrangement of crossings produces different surface textures. Plain weave alternates over and under neighboring warp yarns. Twill arrangements produce diagonal lines, while satin arrangements spread the crossings to create a smoother visible surface. Fiber choice affects softness, strength, moisture absorption, and how a fabric hangs. Cotton fibers grow around seeds and can be spun into yarn after cleaning and preparation. Wool fibers have a crimped structure that contributes to warmth and resilience. Linen fibers come from flax stems and can produce a firm cloth with a distinctive texture. Silk consists of long fibers drawn from cocoons and is known for its smooth appearance. Synthetic fibers are produced from manufactured polymers and can have different lengths and cross sections. Yarn may be twisted more tightly to increase firmness or left more loosely twisted for a softer surface. Dye can be applied to fibers, yarn, or completed cloth. Washing and finishing can change the dimensions and feel of a woven fabric. A selvedge is the finished edge formed along the sides during weaving.
